Shrimad Bhagavat is a narrative of his form, which is displayed by the inner power of God, and

It is different. In this verse, Srila Vyasadeva has clearly explained the difference between these two powers. They say
that the manifest inner power is real, while the external power that appears in the form of the physical world
is transient and like a mirage. In the mirage, there is no real water,
only the illusion of water remains. The real water resides elsewhere. This visible world
seems like a reality, but reality exists in the spiritual world, and
this is merely its shadow (reflection). The ultimate truth is in Vaikuntha Loka (Chidakash),
not in the physical sky.
In the physical universe, everything is relative. The meaning of saying this is
that one truth depends on another. This visible world is made up of the interactions of the three qualities of nature,
and this impermanent world presents the illusion of reality to the deluded mind of the bound soul. Bound souls appear in various forms, including Brahma, Indra,
and higher deities like Chandra. In reality, there is no reality in the manifest world.
But it appears as real. The existence of reality is in Vaikuntha, where
Lord Purushottam remains eternally present with his divine material. The chief engineer of a complex construction work does not participate in the construction work himself, but
he is familiar with every corner of it, because all the work is completed under his direction.
He knows everything about the construction work in direct and indirect ways.
Similarly,
God, being the supreme architect of this visible world, is familiar with every corner of it,
although all the tasks are accomplished by the gods. In this physical creation, from Brahma to a

In this physical world, from the first living being, Brahma, to a tiny ant, all
living beings are eager to obtain some kind of essence through their senses. These sensory pleasures
are called rasa in a technical sense. There are many types of such rasas. In authentic scriptures, the names of the twelve
rasas are enumerated as follows--(1) Raktad (Anger), (2) Adbhut (Wonder), (3) Shringar
(Love), (4) Hasya (Joy), (5) Veera (Valor), (6) Daya (Compassion), (7) Dasya
(Servitude), (8) Sakhya (Friendship), (9) Bhayanak (Fear), (10) Bibhatsa (Disgust),
(19) Shant (Indifference), and (12) Vatsalya (Affection for parents).

The overall essence of all these rasas is affection or love. Basically, such characteristics of love, worship,
service, friendship, affection, and marital love, appear in the form of. When these five are absent,
then love indirectly appears in anger, surprise, laughter, bravery, fear, disgust, etc.
For example, if a man loves a woman, it is the genre of Shringar Rasa. But if such
Obstacles arise in love, it can lead to surprise, anger, shock, or even fear. Sometimes,
The end of the love relationship between two people occurs in brutal murder. Such Rasas are displayed between humans and
between humans and animals. In this world, such exchange of essence
does not happen between humans and animals, nor between humans and any other species. Such exchange of sap takes place only between organisms of the same species. But as far as souls
are concerned, they are qualitatively similar to God. Therefore, in the beginning, the exchange of essence
was with the spiritual being (jivatma) and the spiritual supreme complete, God. This
Spiritual exchange or essence; in the spiritual world, between beings and God, completely
is found.
Therefore, in the Shruti Sanhitas, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is referred to as "Samasta Rasau Ka Nir Sakhot". When a being associates with God and exchanges their natural essence with Him,
then they truly become happy.

These Shruti mantras state that every living being has a natural form, in which God
exchanges a specific type of essence with. Only in a free state, this
original essence can be fully experienced. In the physical world, the experience of rasa (aesthetic emotion) occurs in a distorted form,
which is temporary. Thus, in the physical world, the display of rasa (aesthetic sentiment) occurs in the form of raudra (anger), etc. Therefore, the person who, having attained complete knowledge of these various 'rasas' (essences) in the form of the fundamental elements of activities,
is the one who can understand the diverse forms of the original 'rasas' reflected in the physical world. The scholar, the student, wants to experience the real rasa in its spiritual form. In the beginning, he wants to become one with God. Thus, the ignorant spiritualist, without knowing the various flavors,
without realizing the oneness with the complete soul, cannot go above.
In this verse, it is definitely said that the spiritual essence which is enjoyed
even in a liberated state, can be experienced in the literature of Shrimad Bhagwat,
because it is the ripe fruit of Vedic knowledge. By listening to this divine literature with humility,
a person can attain the desired complete bliss. But a person must be very careful in this matter
that the listening to this message is done with the right intention. The Shrimad Bhagavatam has been completely
obtained only from a suitable source. It is Narad Muni, who brought it from Vaikuntha Loka, who
gave it to his disciple, Shri Vyasadeva. Shri Vyasadev gave this message to his son Shukdev
Goswami, and then he gave it to Maharaj Parikshit just seven days before his death.
Srila Shukadeva Goswami was a liberated soul from his birth. To the extent that he
was liberated in his mother's womb itself, and after birth, he did not have to receive any kind of spiritual education. At the time of birth, no person is skilled from a worldly perspective, nor from a spiritual
perspective. But being a completely free soul, Shri Shukdev Goswami
did not have to follow any kind of development method for spiritual realization.
